performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: How do silence and abrupt changes of speed draw a character with crooked legs?
intro: The first picture is a toy gnome that lurches, halts and shrieks. Listen for the rests: the music is built from bursts of motion and the silences between them. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

cues.title: Bursts and silences
cues.text: The movement opens quietly, about −28 dB below its loudest point, in short bursts from low strings and woodwinds with silence between them. The gnome moves in lurches; count the rests as well as the notes.
cues.evidence: Relative level is −28.3 dB at 0:00 and −28.6 at 0:05 with only 0.8 detected onsets per second, so the opening is quiet and sparse. The low-string and woodwind scoring is from the Philharmonia guide; the report does not identify instruments.

cues.title: A full stop, then a creeping line
cues.text: Around 0:20 the scurrying halts. Upper woodwinds then trace a creeping descending line; the celesta takes it up while strings swoop beneath. The level stays low, between about −26 and −32 dB.
cues.evidence: Relative level is −21.4 dB at 0:15, −29.7 at 0:20 and −26.9 to −32.5 dB from 0:25 to 0:40. The woodwind line, celesta and swooping strings are from the Philharmonia guide; the order and instruments are not identified by the report.

cues.title: A heavy tune joins the scurry
cues.text: From about 0:46 the sound grows louder and heavier. A ponderous idea in the winds is laid over the scurrying figure from the opening, so earlier material returns inside a new, denser texture.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 0:46 (novelty 0.59); relative level rises from −26.3 dB at 0:45 to −21.9 at 0:50. The wind idea combined with the scurrying figure is from the Philharmonia guide.

cues.title: A nutcracker that is lost
cues.text: Hartmann’s drawing is lost. It is thought to show a nutcracker carved as a gnome, with the nuts put into its mouth. Stasov called it a Christmas-tree toy for the Artists’ Club that moved with “savage shrieks”. The Hartmann edge tells the exhibition’s story.
cues.evidence: Stasov’s description is quoted in Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note (https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition); Wikipedia’s article (section “Hartmann’s pictures”) says the sketch is lost and thought to be a nutcracker design. Linked edge: hartmann-pictures--mussorgsky-pictures-1874 in content/influence/romantic.json. The note sits over a quiet dip (−32.7 dB at 0:55).

cues.title: Holding the level
cues.text: From about 1:20, after a dip at 1:15, the level holds near −18 dB for fifteen seconds, unlike the stop-and-start opening. Follow the lurching figure in the low instruments as it keeps interrupting the louder music.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary is 1:24 (novelty 1.00). Relative level is −26.9 dB at 1:15, then −19.5, −17.6 and −17.5 dB at 1:20, 1:25 and 1:30. That the lurching figure continues is a listening suggestion from the score’s structure, not a measured event.

cues.title: The colour turns bright
cues.text: At about 1:45 the sound brightens sharply: shivering high strings and a grotesque wind tune sit far above the bass. This is the movement’s loudest stretch, and it lasts until the sudden drop at 2:10.
cues.evidence: Spectral brightness rises from 944 Hz at 1:40 to 1,921 Hz at 1:45 and stays between 1,620 and 1,870 Hz to 2:05; the loudest 5-second windows are 1:45, 2:00 and 1:55. A 2-second pass of the same audio puts the jump at about 1:45. Shivering strings and wind theme: Philharmonia guide.

cues.title: The floor drops away
cues.text: At 2:10 the sound falls by about fifteen decibels. The creeping idea returns quietly, answered by muted brass. The frantic ending is still twenty seconds away.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −19.4 dB at 2:05 to −33.3 dB at 2:10, the quietest 5-second window, and stays between −27 and −29 dB to 2:25. A 2-second pass puts the fall at about 2:09. The return of the creeping idea and the muted brass are from the Philharmonia guide.

cues.title: The last rush
cues.text: From 2:30 the level climbs and detected attacks leap from two to ten or more every two seconds near 2:36, before a hard stop at 2:40. This is the frantic flourish that finishes the picture.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −27.6 dB at 2:25 to −16.3 at 2:35; onsets per second reach 4.4 at 2:35; a 2-second pass counts 10–11 onsets in each of the windows at 2:36 and 2:38. The level falls to −29.7 dB at 2:40, the final decay.

transitions.title: A full stop opens a quieter idea
transitions.how: The second scurrying phrase ends on an orchestral full stop. After the silence the upper woodwinds begin a slower descending line, higher and thinner than the opening, and the celesta joins with swooping strings. The join rests on contrast of speed, register and colour, not on a modulation: the bursts of motion are replaced by one creeping line.
transitions.evidence: Relative level is −21.4 dB at 0:15 and −29.7 dB at 0:20, then −26 to −32 dB to 0:40; onsets per second go from 2.0 to 1.4. The full stop and the woodwind and celesta line are from the Philharmonia guide; the report cannot time the stop closely.

transitions.title: Opening scurry returns beneath a heavy tune
transitions.how: The creeping line is cut off and the music becomes much heavier. A ponderous idea in the winds is combined with the scurrying figure that began the movement, so the opening material returns inside a denser texture. The key does not matter here as much as weight: the level rises about five decibels and the colour darkens as lower instruments take over.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 0:46 (novelty 0.59); relative level −26.3 dB at 0:45 and −21.9 dB at 0:50. The combination of wind idea and scurry is from the Philharmonia guide; no key change is established by the report.

transitions.title: High strings take over from the bass
transitions.how: After a long, loud middle the colour changes at about 1:45. Shivering high strings and a grotesque wind tune sound far above the bass, and the sound brightens sharply. The lurching low figure that set the pace is no longer in front; register, not rhythm, drives this stretch, which holds its level until the sudden drop at 2:10.
transitions.evidence: Spectral brightness rises from 944 Hz (1:40) to 1,921 Hz (1:45) and stays 1,620–1,870 Hz to 2:05; the loudest windows are 1:45, 2:00 and 1:55. The shivering strings and wind theme are from the Philharmonia guide.

transitions.title: The creeping line comes back, hushed
transitions.how: The loudest music ends abruptly at about 2:10. The creeping descending idea from the second section comes back, now quiet, and muted brass answer it. Returning to the earlier idea after the bright climax gives the movement a frame, and the sudden drop in level makes the return sound like a memory of the earlier creeping line.
transitions.evidence: Relative level falls from −19.4 dB (2:05) to −33.3 dB (2:10), the quietest window, and holds between −27 and −29 dB to 2:25. The return of the creeping idea and the muted brass answer are from the Philharmonia guide.

transitions.title: Hush becomes a frantic rush
transitions.how: From about 2:30 the quiet music is swept up into a quick crescendo. Brighter instruments join, attacks multiply and the sound ends at once: the gnome’s last movement is a flourish, not a cadence. The abruptness leaves the next piece, the second Promenade, to restore the visitor’s steady walk.
transitions.evidence: Relative level rises from −27.6 dB (2:25) to −16.3 dB (2:35); brightness reaches about 2,030 Hz at 2:30–2:35; onsets per second reach 4.4 at 2:35, and a 2-second pass finds 10–11 per window at 2:36–2:38; the level falls at 2:40.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (2:43; this file is 2:41), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The original release is not identified; Musopen and the Free Music Archive are distribution channels.

fields.note: No matrix, take or side identifiers are supplied.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
